analysis.one_liner: Lets unions require workers to join and pay dues, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee it was assigned to; it never received a hearing, a vote, or a House companion.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the part of federal labor law that lets states pass 'right-to-work' laws, which bar unions from requiring workers to join the union or pay dues as a condition of their job. About half of states have such laws. Under the bill, unions and employers in every state could sign contracts requiring union membership, which means more workers paying dues and more unions with money and bargaining power. The bill was read once in the Senate and sent to the committee that handles labor law; nothing happened to it before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in right-to-work states who are covered by union contracts: unions gain members and dues, which strengthens their bargaining power for better pay and conditions. Research consistently shows wages in right-to-work states run lower than in states without them, partly because unions are weaker there. Anyone whose job is made more secure by a stronger union benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Repealing the federal provision that authorizes state right-to-work laws would allow labor agreements in every state to require union membership as a condition of employment, regardless of state law [S2][S3].

This means unions could stop providing free representation to workers who pay nothing, and could collect dues from every worker covered by a union contract, giving unions more resources for bargaining and organizing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in right-to-work states, who would face contracts requiring union membership and the higher labor costs that come with stronger unions. Also, individual workers who do not want the union and would be required to join or pay dues under a union-security contract.

drawbacks.text: Workers who decline to join a union could nonetheless be required to pay dues as a condition of keeping their job, which opponents argue violates the individual worker's freedom of choice [S2].
Employers in the roughly half of states with right-to-work laws would face higher labor costs, which critics say could reduce hiring or business investment in those states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: some workers would be compelled to pay dues they would rather not pay, and employers would face higher labor costs. Supporters counter that unions are legally required to represent every worker under a contract, so letting some workers opt out of paying weakens everyone's bargaining position. Whether compelling dues payments is a fair cost for stronger unions is a genuine values question, not a one-sided one.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and Congress ended with the bill still sitting there.

narrative.text: Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on September 5, 2023, with 17 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents who caucus with Democrats [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; the committee took no further action [S5].
No version of the bill ever received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in right-to-work states keep the status quo, where they can hire workers without union-security requirements. Nonunion workers in those states also keep the choice not to pay dues. The workers the bill was meant to help gained nothing.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sherrod Brown and 16 other Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over labor law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Minority party in the Senate (44 members)
against.what_they_did: No Republican supported the bill, and the party's senators generally back state right-to-work laws that the bill would preempt.

against.name: Business groups supporting right-to-work laws
against.role: Employer associations and right-to-work advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of repealing state right-to-work authority, which they argue protects workers from compelled dues payments and helps states attract employers.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or an allied independent; no Republican cosponsored, and in the Republican-controlled House no companion bill existed [S4][S1].

industries.note: The bill lets unions collect dues from every worker under their contracts, including in the roughly half of states that currently bar it. Stronger dues bases fund more organizing and bargaining, which research links to higher pay for members and nonmembers alike.

Employers would face union-security contracts and the higher labor costs that come with them. Workers who prefer not to belong to a union would also bear a cost in the form of required dues, so the employer's interest here partly tracks those workers' interests.

industries.industry: Temporary and gig-adjacent nonunion workforces in right-to-work states
industries.note: Workers who want union representation would find organizing more effective and higher-paying; workers who do not want it could be required to pay dues anyway.
